cse-2026-2-ga-1.approach: Find the common meaning of the three given words — all three mean *to make something happen faster* — and pick the option that shares it.
concepts: Word meaning from a common thread

steps.title: Common meaning of the given words
steps.body:
- **Expedite**: to make a process happen sooner or more quickly.
- **Hasten**: to make something happen sooner; to hurry.
- **Hurry**: to move or act quickly; to make something go faster.

The shared idea is **speeding something up**.

steps.title: Test each option against "speed up"
steps.body:
- **Accelerate**: to increase speed / make happen sooner — matches.
- **Retard**: to slow down — the *opposite*.
- **Provide**: to supply — unrelated to speed.
- **Disable**: to make unable to work — unrelated.

So the blank is **Accelerate** — option (A).

steps.title: Confirm by substitution
steps.body: "The manager asked the team to **accelerate** the delivery" means the same as *expedite / hasten / hurry* the delivery — the series Expedite, Hasten, Hurry, **Accelerate** is complete.

optionAnalysis.reason: Accelerate = increase speed, the same sense as expedite, hasten and hurry.
Retard means to slow down or delay — an antonym of the given words.
Provide means to supply something; it has nothing to do with speed.
Disable means to make something unable to function; unrelated to speed.

cse-2026-2-ga-1.shortcut: All three cue words are "make it faster"; only one option is a speed word that is not an antonym — Accelerate.
pitfalls: Picking the antonym (Retard) because it is also a "speed" word — the question asks for a similar meaning.
cse-2026-2-ga-1.verification: Substitute: "We must accelerate / expedite / hasten the process" — all read naturally with the same meaning.

cse-2026-2-ga-3.approach: Four independent days with $P(\text{cloudy}) = \tfrac12$ is a binomial experiment. Count the arrangements with exactly three cloudy days and multiply by the probability of one arrangement.

steps.title: Probability of one particular arrangement
steps.body:
For a fixed pattern such as C C C S, independence gives
$$P = \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac{1}{16}.$$
Because $P(\text{cloudy}) = P(\text{sunny}) = \tfrac12$, **every** one of the $2^4 = 16$ patterns has probability $\tfrac{1}{16}$.

steps.title: Count patterns with exactly one sunny day
steps.body: Choose which of the 4 days is sunny: $\binom{4}{3} = \binom{4}{1} = 4$ patterns (SCCC, CSCC, CCSC, CCCS).

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body:
$$P(3\text{ cloudy}, 1\text{ sunny}) = \binom{4}{3}\left(\tfrac12\right)^3\left(\tfrac12\right)^1 = 4 \times \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{4}{16} = \tfrac14.$$
Answer: $\tfrac14$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: $3/4$ is far too large — it would leave only $1/4$ for all the other 12 patterns, which hold $12/16$.
$2/3$ has no basis in a count over $2^4 = 16$ equally likely outcomes.
$3/8 = 6/16$ is the probability of exactly **two** cloudy days ($\binom42 = 6$), not three.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor $\binom43 = 4$ for the position of the sunny day (gives $1/16$, not offered).
Using $\binom42 = 6$ by mistake, which gives $3/8$.
cse-2026-2-ga-3.verification: The five binomial probabilities $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$ over 16 sum to $16/16 = 1$; the "3 cloudy" bar is $4/16$.

cse-2026-2-ga-5.approach: Write the sentence as an implication $R \rightarrow D$ (raining → peacocks dance). An implication is logically equivalent only to its **contrapositive** $\neg D \rightarrow \neg R$; its converse and inverse do not follow.
cse-2026-2-ga-5.given: $R$: it is raining. $D$: peacocks dance. Given: $R \rightarrow D$.

steps.title: Translate each option
steps.body:
- (A) "Peacocks dance **only when** it is raining": $D ightarrow R$ (converse).
- (B) "When peacocks dance, it is raining": $D ightarrow R$ (converse).
- (C) "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining": $
eg D ightarrow 
eg R$ (contrapositive).
- (D) "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance": $
eg R ightarrow 
eg D$ (inverse).

steps.title: Which form must be true?
steps.body:
$R ightarrow D \equiv 
eg R \lor D \equiv D \lor 
eg R \equiv 
eg D ightarrow 
eg R$. So the contrapositive (C) is **necessarily** true: if peacocks are not dancing, it cannot be raining (else they would dance).

The converse and inverse can fail: peacocks may also dance on a sunny day — the sentence says nothing about that case.

steps.title: Counter-example for the other options
steps.body:
Take a dry, sunny day on which peacocks dance. The given sentence is not violated (it only speaks about rainy days), yet
- (A) and (B) claim dancing implies rain — false here;
- (D) claims no rain implies no dancing — false here.
No such world can break (C): if it rained, the peacocks would dance. Hence only (C) is **necessarily** true.

answer.value: **When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining** — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: "Dance only when raining" is $D \rightarrow R$ — the converse; peacocks dancing on a dry day does not contradict the given sentence.
"When peacocks dance, it is raining" is again the converse $D \rightarrow R$, not implied.
Contrapositive $\neg D \rightarrow \neg R$, logically equivalent to $R \rightarrow D$.
"Not raining → not dancing" is the inverse $\neg R \rightarrow \neg D$; it is equivalent to the converse, so it does not follow either.

cse-2026-2-ga-5.shortcut: Flip **and** negate: "raining → dance" becomes "not dance → not raining". Any option that only flips or only negates is wrong.
pitfalls: Reading "A only when B" as $B \rightarrow A$; it means $A \rightarrow B$.
Assuming the sentence also covers what happens when it is not raining.
cse-2026-2-ga-5.verification: Counter-example world: sunny day, peacocks dancing. The given sentence holds (no rain), yet (A), (B) and (D) all fail; (C) still holds.

steps.title: Form the bridge sentence
steps.body: Water is what we take to relieve **thirst**; the need water satisfies is thirst. So $P$ = Thirst.

steps.title: Apply it to food
steps.body:
Food is what we take to relieve **hunger**. So $Q$ = Hunger.

Water : Thirst :: Food : Hunger — option (A).

"Satiated" is the state after eating, not the need food relieves; it does not mirror "thirst".

cse-2026-2-ga-8.approach: The trip is a **Hamiltonian cycle**. For the grid (i), exhibit one. For (ii), use the degree-2 rule: a city with only two highways must use both of them in the cycle — and in (ii) that forces three cycle edges at one city, which is impossible.
cse-2026-2-ga-8.given: Figure (ii) labelled A (top-left), B (top-right), C (inner), D (left), E (bottom). Highways: A–B, A–C, A–D, C–E, D–E, B–E.

Label rows 1–4 (top to bottom) and columns 1–4. Go along the top row $(1,1) \to (1,4)$, then snake back through columns 4, 3, 2 in rows 2–4: $(1,4) \to (2,4) \to (2,2)$ along row 2, down to $(3,2) \to (3,4)$, down to $(4,4) \to (4,1)$, then up column 1: $(4,1) \to (3,1) \to (2,1) \to (1,1)$.
It visits all $16$ cities once and returns to the start, so **(i) is possible**.

steps.title: Figure (ii): cities of degree 2 force their edges
steps.body: B has only highways A–B, B–E; C has only A–C, C–E; D has only A–D, D–E. Each of them must enter and leave on its only two highways, so the cycle must contain **all six** highways.

steps.title: Contradiction at A (and E)
steps.body:
Then A would lie on three cycle edges (A–B, A–C, A–D), but in a cycle every city has exactly 2. (A 5-city cycle also has only 5 edges, not 6.) So **no such trip exists for (ii)**.

Trip possible for (i) but not for (ii) — option (A).

scene.caption: A would need 3 cycle edges — impossible

Reversed: (i) does have a tour, and (ii) does not.
(ii) has no tour: B, C, D force all six highways into the cycle, giving A degree 3.
(i) does have a tour — an explicit one is shown in step 1.

cse-2026-2-cs-1.approach: Name the special person $y$. "There is a person" gives $\exists y$ outermost; "everyone else" gives $\forall x$ with $x \ne y$. For each such $x$: $x$ knows $y$ and $y$ does not know $x$.

steps.title: Translate the inner condition
steps.body:
For a fixed other person $x 
e y$:
- "that person is known by everyone else" → $M(x, y)$ ($x$ knows $y$);
- "does not know anyone else" → $
eg M(y, x)$.
Combined: $(x 
e y) ightarrow (M(x,y) \land 
eg M(y,x))$. The implication restricts the claim to people other than $y$ — the right form for a universal.

steps.title: Attach the quantifiers
steps.body: One fixed person works against **all** others: $(\exists y)(\forall x)\,((x \ne y) \rightarrow (M(x,y) \land \neg M(y,x)))$ — option (A). The order $\exists y\,\forall x$ matters: the same $y$ must work for every $x$.

steps.title: Why the other prefixes fail
steps.body:
- $\forall y\,\exists x$: each person has *some* other person — no single special person.
- $\exists y\,\exists x$: choosing $x = y$ makes the implication vacuously true, so the formula says nothing.
- $\forall y\,\forall x$: demands that everyone is known by and knows no one else — contradictory as soon as there are two people.
Only $\exists y\,\forall x$ (option A) fits.

$\forall y\,\exists x$ says every person has *someone* who knows them and whom they do not know — no single special person.
$\exists y\,\exists x$ with an implication is trivially true (pick $x = y$, making the antecedent false); it says nothing about everyone.
$\forall y\,\forall x$ demands this of **every** person, which is self-contradictory for two people ($M(x,y)$ and $\neg M(x,y)$).

cse-2026-2-cs-3.approach: Use the definition: $M$ **decides** $L$ when $M$ halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings of $L$ and rejecting all others. Since "rejects" means halting in the reject state, "accepts every $w \in L$ and rejects every $w \notin L$" says the same thing.

steps.title: What "decides" requires
steps.body:
On every input $w \in \{0,1\}^*$ the machine must halt, and
- $w \in L \Rightarrow M$ accepts;
- $w \notin L \Rightarrow M$ rejects (halts in the reject state).
Both halves are needed; the halting requirement is implied by them, because accepting and rejecting are both halting outcomes.

steps.title: Options that state only part of it
steps.body:
- (A) Halting on all inputs alone does not say *which* strings are accepted — $M$ might decide a different language.
- (B) Accepting all of $L$ still allows $M$ to accept or loop on strings outside $L$ (it only gives $L \subseteq L(M)$).
- (C) Rejecting all of $\{0,1\}^* - L$ still allows $M$ to reject or loop on strings in $L$.

steps.title: The equivalent statement
steps.body: (D) Accepting every $w \in L$ and rejecting every $w \notin L$ means $M$ halts on every input (accept and reject are both halting states) with the correct verdict — exactly the definition of "$M$ decides $L$". Option (D).

answer.value: **$M$ accepts all strings in $L$ and rejects all strings in $\{0,1\}^* - L$** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: Halting on all inputs is necessary but not sufficient: a machine that rejects everything halts on all inputs yet does not decide a non-empty $L$.
Only half the definition: strings outside $L$ could be accepted or cause looping (a recogniser need not even do that).
Only the other half: strings in $L$ could be rejected or loop.
Accept on $L$ + reject on the complement = halts on every input with the correct answer — the definition of deciding.

cse-2026-2-cs-3.shortcut: Decider = total + correct. Only (D) pins down the verdict on every string; totality then follows automatically.
pitfalls: Treating "halts on all inputs" as the definition of a decider — it must also give the right answer.
Confusing "decides" with "recognises" (accepts exactly $L$, may loop outside).
cse-2026-2-cs-3.verification: Counter-example to (A): $L = \{0\}$ and $M$ rejecting every input — $M$ halts everywhere but rejects $0 \in L$, so it does not decide $L$, while (D) correctly fails for this $M$.

cse-2026-2-cs-4.approach: Pattern-match the density against the standard forms: only the normal density has the shape $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ on the whole real line. Reading off $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and checking the constant confirms it.

steps.title: Write the general normal density
steps.body:
A normal random variable $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has

cse-2026-2-cs-12.approach: Ask which protocol must work before the host knows any server address (or even its own IP address): only then is broadcast unavoidable. That is DHCP; the others are client–server application protocols over a TCP connection to a known address.

steps.title: The rest of the exchange
steps.body: After the OFFER, the client **broadcasts DHCPREQUEST** as well (so that all servers that made offers learn which one was accepted), and a server may broadcast its OFFER/ACK when the client cannot yet receive unicast. So DHCP may need to broadcast — option **(C)**.

cse-2026-2-cs-13.approach: An algorithm is preemptive if it can take the CPU away from a running process. Check whether each algorithm has (or can have) such a trigger; FCFS by definition runs each job to completion in arrival order.

steps.title: SRTF and Round Robin are preemptive by definition

steps.body: Priority scheduling can be **preemptive** (a higher-priority arrival takes the CPU) or non-preemptive. So it *can* be preemptive.

steps.body: FCFS dispatches processes in arrival order and lets each run until it terminates or blocks — there is no event on which it would preempt. Adding preemption (e.g. a time slice) turns it into Round Robin. So FCFS **cannot** be preemptive — option **(B)**.

cse-2026-2-cs-14.approach: Simplify each function to a standard form first: $2^{\log_2 n} = n$ and $\log(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$ (Stirling). Then the order of $\log n,\ n^{1/3},\ n,\ n\log n$ is immediate.

steps.body: With base 2, $2^{\log_2 n} = n$. So this function is linear.

steps.title: Simplify log(n!)
steps.body: Upper bound: $\log(n!) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log i \le n\log n$. Lower bound: the largest $n/2$ terms are each $\ge \log(n/2)$, so $\log(n!) \ge \frac{n}{2}\log\frac{n}{2}$. Hence $\log(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$.

steps.title: log n versus n^{1/3}

$$\log n \;\prec\; n^{1/3} \;\prec\; 2^{\log n} = n \;\prec\; \log(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$$

cse-2026-2-cs-17.approach: Integrate term by term over the symmetric interval $[-1,1]$: the odd term $-ax$ integrates to $0$, so $I(a)$ is a constant. Then read each statement against that constant.
concepts: Odd and even functions on a symmetric interval

steps.title: Add them
steps.body:
$$I(a) = 2 - a\cdot 0 + 2 = 4 \quad\text{for every real } a.$$
So $I(a)$ does not depend on $a$ (A true, B false), $I(a) = 4 > 0$ for every $a$ (C true), and it is never negative (D false).

optionAnalysis.reason: The $a$-term is $-a\int_{-1}^{1}x\,dx = -a\cdot 0 = 0$, so $I(a) = 4$ whatever $a$ is.
Would need $\int_{-1}^{1} x\,dx \ne 0$; but $x$ is odd on a symmetric interval, so its integral is $0$.
$I(a) = 4 > 0$ for every $a$, so certainly some $a$ (e.g. $a = 0$) gives a positive value.
$I(a)$ is always $4$, never negative. Choosing a large $a$ does not help because the $a$-term vanishes.

cse-2026-2-cs-17.shortcut: On $[-1,1]$ odd terms vanish: keep only the even part $3x^2 + 1$, whose integral is $2\int_0^1(3x^2+1)\,dx = 2(1+1) = 4$.
pitfalls: Thinking a parameter in the integrand must make the value vary with it — here it multiplies an odd function.
Integrating $3x^2$ as $x^2$ or forgetting the factor from both halves of the interval.
cse-2026-2-cs-17.verification: Direct antiderivative: $F(x) = x^3 - \tfrac{a}{2}x^2 + x$; $F(1) - F(-1) = \left(2 - \tfrac a2\right) - \left(-2 - \tfrac a2\right) = 4$.

cse-2026-2-cs-18.approach: Convert the four 4-bit patterns to decimals; 4-bit two's complement holds only $[-8, 7]$, so an operation overflows exactly when its true result leaves that range (equivalently, two same-sign operands give a result of the other sign).

steps.title: A: N1 + N2
steps.body: $-5 + (-3) = -8$, inside the range. Bitwise: $1011 + 1101 = 1\,1000$, keep $1000 = -8$ (negative + negative = negative). **No overflow.**

steps.title: B: N2 + N3
steps.body: $-3 + (-6) = -9 < -8$. Bitwise: $1101 + 1010 = 1\,0111$, keep $0111 = +7$: two negatives gave a positive. **Overflow.**

steps.title: C: N3 − N4
steps.body: $-6 - (-7) = +1$, inside the range. Hardware adds the negation: $-N_4 = 0111$, and $1010 + 0111 = 1\,0001$, keep $0001 = 1$. Operands of opposite sign can never overflow. **No overflow.**

steps.title: D: N1 + N4
steps.body: $-5 + (-7) = -12 < -8$. Bitwise: $1011 + 1001 = 1\,0100$, keep $0100 = +4$: two negatives gave a positive. **Overflow.**

answer.value: Overflow occurs for **$N_2 + N_3$ and $N_1 + N_4$** — options (B) and (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: $-5 + (-3) = -8$ is exactly the most negative 4-bit value ($1000$), so it fits. Treating $-8$ as out of range is the trap.
$-3 + (-6) = -9 < -8$; the 4-bit sum $0111 = +7$ has the wrong sign.
$-6 - (-7) = +1$; adding $1010 + 0111$ gives $0001$. The end carry out is discarded and is not an overflow.
$-5 + (-7) = -12 < -8$; the 4-bit sum $0100 = +4$ has the wrong sign.

cse-2026-2-cs-18.shortcut: All four numbers are negative. Sums of two negatives overflow when the magnitudes add to more than $8$: $5+3 = 8$ (fits), $3+6 = 9$ and $5+7 = 12$ (overflow). A difference of two negatives cannot overflow.
pitfalls: Calling a carry out of the MSB an overflow — in two's complement, overflow means the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of it.
Forgetting that $-8$ is representable in 4 bits, so $N_1 + N_2$ is fine.
Reading the patterns as unsigned numbers.
cse-2026-2-cs-18.verification: Carry rule: for $N_2+N_3$ ($1101+1010$) the carry into bit 3 is $0$ and the carry out is $1$ — they differ, overflow. For $N_1+N_2$ ($1011+1101$) both carries are $1$ — no overflow.

cse-2026-2-cs-19.approach: A grammar is ambiguous if one string has two different parse trees (or leftmost derivations). Look for a short witness string in each grammar; for the others, argue that each step of the derivation is forced.

steps.title: A and D are unambiguous
steps.body:
- (A) $S \to aSb \mid \epsilon$: every sentence is $a^nb^n$, and the only derivation applies $S \to aSb$ exactly $n$ times then $S \to \epsilon$. Each step is forced, so exactly one parse tree.
- (D) $S \to aS \mid \epsilon$: generates $a^n$ by $n$ uses of $S \to aS$ then $S \to \epsilon$ — again a single forced chain.

steps.title: B is ambiguous
steps.body:
For $id + id * id$:

1. $E \Rightarrow E + E \Rightarrow id + E \Rightarrow id + E * E \Rightarrow id + id * id$ (the $*$ is below the $+$)
2. $E \Rightarrow E * E \Rightarrow E + E * E \Rightarrow id + E * E \Rightarrow id + id * id$ (the $+$ is below the $*$)

Two different leftmost derivations, two parse trees — the grammar fixes neither precedence nor associativity.

scene.title: (B) two trees for id + id * id

steps.title: C is ambiguous
steps.body:
For the one-symbol string $a$:

1. $S \Rightarrow aS \Rightarrow a$ (using $S \to \epsilon$)
2. $S \Rightarrow Sa \Rightarrow a$ (using $S \to \epsilon$)

The roots use different productions, so the parse trees differ. ($S \to aS \mid Sa$ lets the $a$'s be added from either side.)

optionAnalysis.reason: Every string $a^nb^n$ has exactly one derivation ($n$ times $S \to aSb$, then $S \to \epsilon$); no choice ever arises.
$id + id * id$ has two leftmost derivations (start with $E \to E+E$ or with $E \to E*E$).
The string $a$ has two parse trees: $S \to aS$ or $S \to Sa$ at the root, each finished by $S \to \epsilon$.
Right-linear: each $a^n$ is produced by the unique chain $S \to aS$ ($n$ times), $S \to \epsilon$.

cse-2026-2-cs-19.shortcut: A production with the nonterminal on **both** sides of a symbol, or two productions that can build the same string from opposite ends ($S \to aS \mid Sa$), is a red flag — try the shortest string first.
pitfalls: Thinking A is ambiguous because it is not regular — ambiguity and regularity are unrelated.
Missing C: the language is just $a^*$, but the grammar (not the language) is what is ambiguous.
cse-2026-2-cs-19.verification: Count parse trees for $a^2$ in C: root $aS$ or $Sa$, and the inner $S$ for $a$ again has 2 choices, giving more than one tree; in D, $a^2$ has only $S \Rightarrow aS \Rightarrow aaS \Rightarrow aa$.

cse-2026-2-cs-21.approach: A $2\times 2$ system has infinitely many solutions only when the coefficient determinant is $0$ **and** the equations are consistent (the two rows are proportional including the right-hand side). Solve for $a$ first, then $b$.

steps.title: Singular coefficient matrix
steps.body:
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 16 & a \end{bmatrix} = a^2 - 16 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 4 \text{ or } a = -4$$
If $a^2 \ne 16$ the solution is unique, so multiple solutions force $a = \pm 4$.

steps.title: Consistency fixes b
steps.body:
The two equations must be multiples of each other: $\dfrac{a}{16} = \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{b}{24}$.

- $a = 4$: $\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{b}{24} \Rightarrow b = 6$. (Check: $4x + y = 6$ times $4$ gives $16x + 4y = 24$ ✓)
- $a = -4$: $-\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{b}{24} \Rightarrow b = -6$. (Check: $-4x + y = -6$ times $-4$ gives $16x - 4y = 24$ ✓)

steps.title: Product
steps.body: Either way $ab = 4 \times 6 = 24$ or $ab = (-4)\times(-6) = 24$. So $ab = \mathbf{24}$.

cse-2026-2-cs-21.shortcut: Multiply the first equation by $a$: $a^2x + ay = ab$. For it to coincide with $16x + ay = 24$ you need $a^2 = 16$ and $ab = 24$ — the product drops out directly.
pitfalls: Stopping at $\det = 0$: with the wrong $b$ the system is inconsistent (no solution).
Taking only $a = 4$ and worrying the answer is ambiguous — both roots give the same product.
cse-2026-2-cs-21.verification: With $a = 4, b = 6$: every point on $y = 6 - 4x$ satisfies both equations, e.g. $(0, 6)$: $16\cdot 0 + 4\cdot 6 = 24$ ✓ and $(1, 2)$: $16 + 8 = 24$ ✓.

cse-2026-2-cs-22.approach: A merge of sorted $L$ and $R$ is void exactly when $\max(L) \le \min(R)$, i.e. the last element of $L$ does not exceed the first of $R$. Walk the 7 merges of top-down merge sort and test that one comparison each time.

steps.title: Void test
steps.body: The merge outputs $L$ then $R$ unchanged iff every element of $L$ is $\le$ every element of $R$, i.e. $L_{\text{last}} \le R_{\text{first}}$ (both runs are sorted). The 7 merges are the 7 internal nodes of the recursion tree: 4 merges of singletons, 2 of pairs, 1 final.

steps.title: Final merge and count
steps.body:
$L = [7, 8, 10, 19]$, $R = [25, 31, 35, 41]$: $19 \le 25$, so the output is $L$ followed by $R$ — **void**.

Void merges: $[8]+[19]$, $[25]+[31]$ and the final merge, a total of $\mathbf{3}$.

cse-2026-2-cs-22.shortcut: Void at a node $\iff$ the left half's maximum $\le$ the right half's minimum. Left/right maxima-minima: $(10,7)$ ✗, $(8,19)$ ✓, $(41,35)$ ✗, $(25,31)$ ✓, $(10,8)$ ✗, $(41,25)$ ✗, $(19,25)$ ✓ → 3.
pitfalls: Judging a merge by the original unsorted halves: the pair merge uses the sorted runs $[7,10]$ and $[8,19]$.
Missing the final merge: its halves are already split cleanly ($19 < 25$).
cse-2026-2-cs-22.verification: Independent check with maxima/minima of the original halves: final merge compares $\max\{10,7,8,19\} = 19$ with $\min\{41,35,25,31\} = 25$ → void; the right pair merge compares $\max\{41,35\} = 41$ with $\min\{25,31\} = 25$ → not void.

cse-2026-2-cs-23.approach: Count the 0-bits of the mask (host bits $h$); the block has $2^h$ addresses, of which the all-0s (network) and all-1s (broadcast) host parts cannot be assigned to interfaces.

steps.title: Count host bits
steps.body: Ones: $8 + 8 + 4 = 20$, so this is a /20 network (network + subnet part). Zeros: $32 - 20 = 12$ host bits.

steps.title: Usable addresses
steps.body:
Host part has $2^{12} = 4096$ patterns. Remove the all-0s pattern (network address) and the all-1s pattern (directed broadcast):

$$2^{12} - 2 = 4096 - 2 = 4094$$

cse-2026-2-cs-23.shortcut: Third octet $240 = 256 - 16$, so the block spans $16$ values of the third octet: $16 \times 256 = 4096$ addresses, minus 2 → $4094$.
pitfalls: Answering 4096 by forgetting the network and broadcast addresses.
Counting host bits as 4 (from 240 alone) and forgetting the fully-zero last octet.

cse-2026-2-cs-25.approach: Scan each whitespace-separated chunk with longest match: an $id$ must start with a letter and may then absorb letters and digits, while a $number$ is a maximal run of digits. So a chunk splits only where a digit run is followed by a letter.

steps.title: How a chunk is cut
steps.body:
- Starting at a letter: $id$ takes every following letter **and** digit, so $x1$, $zz5$, $AaYcD$ are one token each.
- Starting at a digit: $number$ takes the digits; the first letter ends it and starts a new $id$. So $23mm \to 23,\ mm$.
- $ws$ separates chunks and is not counted.

steps.title: First five chunks
steps.body:
| chunk | tokens | count |
|---|---|---|
| x1 | id(x1) | 1 |
| 23mm | number(23), id(mm) | 2 |
| 78 | number(78) | 1 |
| y | id(y) | 1 |
| 7z | number(7), id(z) | 2 |

Running total: $1+2+1+1+2 = 7$.

steps.title: Last four chunks
steps.body:
| chunk | tokens | count |
|---|---|---|
| zz5 | id(zz5) | 1 |
| 14A | number(14), id(A) | 2 |
| 8H | number(8), id(H) | 2 |
| AaYcD | id(AaYcD) | 1 |

Subtotal $1+2+2+1 = 6$; total $7 + 6 = \mathbf{13}$.

Treating $23mm$ as one token or as an error — longest match gives $number$ then $id$.
Counting whitespace as tokens.

cse-2026-2-cs-26.approach: The Jaccard coefficient is $\frac{|T_1 \cap T_2|}{|T_1 \cup T_2|} \ge 0$, with equality iff the two trees share no edge. So the question is whether $K_n$ ($n > 4$) has two **edge-disjoint** spanning trees — exhibit them.

steps.title: Lower bound 0
steps.body:
For edge sets $T_1, T_2$ the numerator $|T_1 \cap T_2| \ge 0$ and the denominator $|T_1 \cup T_2| \ge n - 1 > 0$, so $J \ge 0$, and $J = 0 \iff T_1 \cap T_2 = \varnothing$.

Edge count allows it: two disjoint trees need $2(n-1)$ edges, and $\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \ge 2(n-1) \iff n \ge 4$.

steps.title: Build two disjoint trees
steps.body:
Label the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$.

- $T_1 = \{v_1v_3, v_1v_4, \dots, v_1v_n\} \cup \{v_2v_3\}$: a star at $v_1$ on $v_3..v_n$, with $v_2$ hung on $v_3$. Edges: $(n-2) + 1 = n-1$, connected ⇒ spanning tree.
- $T_2 = \{v_2v_1, v_2v_4, \dots, v_2v_n\} \cup \{v_3v_4\}$: a star at $v_2$ on $v_1, v_4..v_n$, with $v_3$ hung on $v_4$. Edges: $1 + (n-3) + 1 = n-1$, connected ⇒ spanning tree.

No edge is shared ($v_1v_2$, $v_3v_4$ and $v_2v_k$ are not in $T_1$).

steps.title: Compute J
steps.body:
$$J(T_1, T_2) = \frac{|T_1 \cap T_2|}{|T_1 \cup T_2|} = \frac{0}{2(n-1)} = 0$$
Since $J \ge 0$ always, the lowest possible value is $\mathbf{0}$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac1n$ does not even arise naturally: one shared edge gives $\frac{1}{2n-3}$, and edge-disjoint trees give $0$, which is smaller.
$\frac{1}{2n-3}$ is the value when the trees share exactly **one** edge ($|\cap| = 1$, $|\cup| = 2(n-1) - 1$); it is not the minimum because sharing no edge is possible.
$K_n$ with $n > 4$ has two edge-disjoint spanning trees, so the intersection can be empty and $J = 0$.
$\frac{1}{n-1}$ would be $|\cap| = 1$ over a union of only $n-1$ edges — impossible for two different trees, and anyway larger than $0$.

cse-2026-2-cs-26.shortcut: Nash-Williams/Tutte: $K_n$ contains $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ edge-disjoint spanning trees, which is $\ge 2$ for $n \ge 4$. Disjoint ⇒ $J = 0$.
pitfalls: Assuming every two spanning trees must share an edge.
Computing the Jaccard value for trees sharing one edge ($\frac{1}{2n-3}$) and stopping there.
cse-2026-2-cs-26.verification: In $K_5$: $T_1 = \{13, 14, 15, 23\}$ and $T_2 = \{12, 24, 25, 34\}$ each have 4 edges, reach all 5 vertices, and share nothing; $J = 0/8 = 0$.

cse-2026-2-cs-27.approach: In a DAG, relax edges in topological order: one topological sort plus one relaxation per edge gives all shortest-path lengths in $\Theta(m + n)$, works even with negative weights, and no algorithm can avoid reading the edges.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
1. Topologically sort $G$ (DFS finishing times or Kahn's algorithm): $\Theta(m + n)$.
2. Set $d[s] = 0$, $d[v] = \infty$ otherwise.
3. For each vertex $u$ in topological order, for each edge $(u, v)$: $d[v] = \min(d[v],\, d[u] + w(u, v))$.

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body: Every path into $v$ uses only vertices that come before $v$ in topological order. When $u$ is processed, all of its predecessors were already processed, so $d[u]$ is final; relaxing $u$'s out-edges therefore propagates exact distances (induction along the order). Negative weights are fine — a DAG has no cycles at all.

steps.title: Running time and lower bound
steps.body:
Sorting: $\Theta(m + n)$. Relaxation: each vertex once and each edge once, $\Theta(n + m)$. Total $\Theta(m + n)$.

It cannot be beaten in the worst case: any edge that is not read could be the one that shortens a path, so $\Omega(m)$ edge inspections (and $\Omega(n)$ outputs) are needed.

optionAnalysis.reason: Topological sort + one relaxation per edge; linear and optimal.
Dijkstra with a Fibonacci heap — slower than necessary, and it is not even correct if some weights are negative, which a weighted DAG allows.
Bellman–Ford's $\Theta(nm)$ handles general graphs; on a DAG a single pass in topological order already suffices.
$\Theta(n^3)$ is Floyd–Warshall (all pairs) — far more than a single source needs.

cse-2026-2-cs-27.shortcut: DAG + single source ⇒ “topo-sort then relax” ⇒ linear time. Remember it as the DAG-SP algorithm from CLRS §24.2.
pitfalls: Reaching for Dijkstra by habit; it is neither the fastest here nor safe with negative weights.
Choosing Bellman–Ford because weights may be negative — the acyclicity removes the need for $n-1$ passes.
cse-2026-2-cs-27.verification: Sanity check of optimality: the input itself has size $\Theta(m + n)$, so a $\Theta(m + n)$ algorithm is the best possible order of growth.

cse-2026-2-cs-28.approach: Let $d_k = A[k+1] - A[k]$. The condition says $d_i > d_j$ whenever $i > j$, i.e. the difference sequence is strictly increasing — which is equivalent to checking only **adjacent** pairs $d_{k+1} > d_k$. One linear scan does it, and every element must be read.

steps.title: Rewrite the condition
steps.body:
With $d_k = A[k+1] - A[k]$ for $k = 1, \dots, n-1$, the condition is
$$\forall\, i > j:\ d_i > d_j \iff d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_{n-1}.$$
Checking $d_{k+1} > d_k$ for $k = 1, \dots, n-2$ suffices: by transitivity $d_j < d_{j+1} < \dots < d_i$ for any $i > j$.

steps.title: Linear algorithm
steps.body: Scan $k = 1$ to $n-2$, compute $d_k$ and $d_{k+1}$, and reject as soon as $d_{k+1} \le d_k$; accept at the end. That is $n - 2$ comparisons and $O(n)$ time.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: Any correct algorithm must read every $A[k]$ in the worst case. Take a valid array such as $A[k] = k^2$ (differences $3, 5, 7, \dots$). If some $A[k]$ is never read, changing it by a large enough amount changes $d_{k-1}$ and $d_k$ in opposite directions and breaks the strict increase — but the algorithm would give the same answer. So $\Omega(n)$, and the worst case is $\Theta(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Adjacent-difference scan is $O(n)$, and the adversary argument gives $\Omega(n)$.
$\Theta(\log n)$ would mean reading only a few elements; any unread element can break the property, so this is impossible.
Sorting the differences is unnecessary — their order must already be the index order, which a scan checks.
$\Theta(n^2)$ is the literal check over all pairs $(i, j)$; transitivity reduces it to adjacent pairs.

cse-2026-2-cs-28.shortcut: “For all $i > j$, $f(i) > f(j)$” = “$f$ strictly increasing” = check neighbours only ⇒ one pass ⇒ $\Theta(n)$.
pitfalls: Implementing the quantifier literally with two nested loops.
Thinking binary search applies because the differences are “sorted” — that is what has to be verified, not assumed.
cse-2026-2-cs-28.verification: Example $A = [1, 2, 4, 7, 11]$: $d = 1, 2, 3, 4$ (increasing) ✓. Change $A[3]$ from $4$ to $10$: $d = 1, 8, -3, 4$ — the scan rejects at $k = 2$ ($-3 \le 8$).

cse-2026-2-cs-29.approach: $T[i][j]$ depends on its **upper** neighbour $T[i-1][j]$ and **left** neighbour $T[i][j-1]$. An evaluation order is correct iff both are final before $T[i][j]$ is written. Check that for row-major order (B1) and anti-diagonal order (B2).

steps.title: Dependencies
steps.body:
Row 0 and column 0 are base cases with value 1, and both algorithms start with every entry equal to 1, so the boundary is already correct and is never overwritten (both loops start at $1$).

For $1 \le i, j \le n$: $T[i][j]$ needs $T[i-1][j]$ (one row up) and $T[i][j-1]$ (one column left). Each is a boundary cell or an interior cell with smaller $i + j$.

steps.title: B1: row by row
steps.body:
When B1 computes $T[i][j]$:

- $T[i-1][j]$: row $i-1$ was finished in the previous iteration of the outer loop (or is row 0).
- $T[i][j-1]$: computed just before in the same row (or is column 0).

Both are final, so each entry is computed once with correct inputs. **B1 is correct.** (For $n = 3$: $T[1][\cdot] = 5, 17, 53$; $T[2][\cdot] = 13, 73, 325$; $T[3][\cdot] = 29, 233, 1349$.)

scene.caption: Row-major order: each row uses the finished row above

steps.title: B2: anti-diagonal by anti-diagonal
steps.body:
In pass $s$ B2 writes exactly the interior cells with $i + j = s$ (the $If$ filters the $n^2$ pairs). Their inputs $T[i-1][j]$ and $T[i][j-1]$ have index sum $s - 1$: either boundary cells, or interior cells written in pass $s-1$. By induction on $s$, every pass reads only final values.

Every interior cell has $2 \le i + j \le 2n$, so each is written in exactly one pass. **B2 is correct** too (it just wastes time: $\Theta(n^3)$ iterations).

scene.caption: Pass s = 4 writes (1,3), (2,2), (3,1) from the finished diagonal s = 3

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both algorithms respect the dependency order (each is a topological order of the DAG “up-neighbour, left-neighbour → cell”), so both compute the correct table: option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Row-major order and anti-diagonal order both compute every cell after its up and left neighbours.
Assumes the anti-diagonal sweep reads unfinished cells; but the inputs of a cell on diagonal $s$ lie on diagonal $s - 1$, finished in the previous pass.
Assumes row-major order is wrong; the up-neighbour is in the finished previous row and the left-neighbour was just computed.
Confuses inefficiency ($B_2$ loops $\Theta(n^3)$ times) with incorrectness; neither algorithm ever uses a stale value.

cse-2026-2-cs-29.shortcut: Any order in which $(i-1, j)$ and $(i, j-1)$ come before $(i, j)$ works. Row-major: yes. Increasing $i + j$: yes (both neighbours have sum $i + j - 1$). ⇒ both correct.
pitfalls: Thinking the initial 1s are a bug — they are exactly the base cases for row 0 and column 0.
Equating “slow” with “incorrect” for B2.

cse-2026-2-cs-30.approach: Plot the eight minterms on a 4-variable K-map: they fill the two whole rows where $B = 0$, which is a single octet. An octet over 4 variables eliminates three variables, so the minimal SOP is one literal.
cse-2026-2-cs-30.given: $F(A,B,C,D) = \Sigma m(0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11)$, with $A$ the MSB and $D$ the LSB.

steps.title: Write the minterms in binary
steps.body:
| minterms | $ABCD$ | common bits |
|---|---|---|
| $0,1,2,3$ | $00\,xx$ | $A=0,\ B=0$ |
| $8,9,10,11$ | $10\,xx$ | $A=1,\ B=0$ |

In all eight minterms $B = 0$; $A$, $C$, $D$ take every combination ($2^3 = 8$ of them).

steps.title: Group the octet on the K-map
steps.body: Rows $AB = 00$ and $AB = 10$ are adjacent on the K-map (the first and last rows in Gray order $00, 01, 11, 10$ wrap around). Together they form one rectangle of $2 \times 4 = 8$ cells — an **octet**.

steps.title: Read off the literal
steps.body:
Inside the octet $A$ changes ($0$ and $1$), $C$ changes and $D$ changes; only $B$ stays $0$. So the octet is the single literal $B'$:

$$F = B'.$$

One implicant with one literal cannot be simplified further, so this is the minimal SOP — option **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $A'+B'+C'+D'$ is $0$ only for $m_{15}$, so it is $1$ on 15 minterms — e.g. $m_4$ ($0100$), which is not in $F$.
Exactly the minterms with $B=0$: $0$–$3$ and $8$–$11$.
$A'B' + AB$ covers $0$–$3$ and $12$–$15$; it misses $8$–$11$ and wrongly includes $12$–$15$ (confusing $AB=10$ with $AB=11$).
$A'$ covers $0$–$7$: it includes $4$–$7$ and misses $8$–$11$.

cse-2026-2-cs-30.shortcut: $\{0,\dots,3\} \cup \{8,\dots,11\}$ are exactly the numbers $0$–$15$ whose bit of weight $4$ (that is $B$) is $0$, so $F = B'$ immediately.

Reading the row order as binary ($00,01,10,11$) instead of Gray order.
cse-2026-2-cs-30.verification: Algebra: $\Sigma m(0..3) = A'B'$ and $\Sigma m(8..11) = AB'$, so $F = A'B' + AB' = (A'+A)B' = B'$.

cse-2026-2-cs-31.approach: Build the canonical LR(0) item sets and look for states that contain both a complete item $X \to \alpha\cdot$ and an item with a terminal after the dot. In LR(0) a reduce item fills the whole ACTION row, so every such state is one shift-reduce conflict; the $\epsilon$-productions make this happen often.
cse-2026-2-cs-31.given: Augmented grammar: $S' \to S$, $S \to ACB$, $A \to aA \mid \epsilon$, $C \to cC \mid \epsilon$, $B \to bB \mid b$.

steps.title: Start state I0
steps.body:
$I_0 = \text{closure}\{S' \to \cdot S\} = \{S' \to \cdot S,\ S \to \cdot ACB,\ A \to \cdot aA,\ A \to \cdot\}$.

$A \to \cdot$ is a complete item (the $\epsilon$-production), so LR(0) puts **reduce $A \to \epsilon$** in every column of row $I_0$; $A \to \cdot aA$ asks to **shift $a$**. Conflict #1.

steps.title: Follow A: states I2, I3, I4
steps.body:
- $I_2 = \text{goto}(I_0, A) = \{S \to A\cdot CB,\ C \to \cdot cC,\ C \to \cdot\}$: shift $c$ vs reduce $C \to \epsilon$ — conflict #2.
- $I_3 = \text{goto}(I_0, a) = \{A \to a\cdot A,\ A \to \cdot aA,\ A \to \cdot\}$: shift $a$ vs reduce $A \to \epsilon$ — conflict #3. ($\text{goto}(I_3, a) = I_3$.)
- $I_4 = \text{goto}(I_3, A) = \{A \to aA\cdot\}$: reduce only.
- $I_1 = \text{goto}(I_0, S) = \{S' \to S\cdot\}$: accept.

steps.title: Follow C: states I5, I6, I7
steps.body:
- $I_6 = \text{goto}(I_2, c) = \{C \to c\cdot C,\ C \to \cdot cC,\ C \to \cdot\}$: shift $c$ vs reduce $C \to \epsilon$ — conflict #4. ($\text{goto}(I_6, c) = I_6$.)
- $I_7 = \text{goto}(I_6, C) = \{C \to cC\cdot\}$: reduce only.
- $I_5 = \text{goto}(I_2, C) = \{S \to AC\cdot B,\ B \to \cdot bB,\ B \to \cdot b\}$: only shift $b$ — no complete item, no conflict.

steps.title: Follow B: states I8, I9, I10
steps.body:
- $I_9 = \text{goto}(I_5, b) = \{B \to b\cdot B,\ B \to b\cdot,\ B \to \cdot bB,\ B \to \cdot b\}$: $B \to b\cdot$ is complete while $B \to \cdot bB$, $B \to \cdot b$ want to shift $b$ — conflict #5. ($\text{goto}(I_9, b) = I_9$.)
- $I_{10} = \text{goto}(I_9, B) = \{B \to bB\cdot\}$ and $I_8 = \text{goto}(I_5, B) = \{S \to ACB\cdot\}$: reduce only.

steps.title: Count the conflicts
steps.body:
The collection has 11 states $I_0, \dots, I_{10}$. The states with a shift-reduce conflict are $I_0, I_2, I_3, I_6, I_9$:

$$1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5.$$

There are no reduce-reduce conflicts (no state has two complete items). Answer: **5** — option **(D)**.

scene.caption: 5 states with a shift-reduce conflict: I0, I2, I3, I6, I9.

optionAnalysis.reason: 2 counts only the two states that start an $\epsilon$-loop ($I_0$, $I_2$) and misses $I_3$, $I_6$ (the $\epsilon$-item reappears after shifting $a$ / $c$) and $I_9$.
3 counts only the $\epsilon$-related conflicts of one kind (e.g. $I_0, I_2, I_9$) and forgets that $I_3$ and $I_6$ also contain $A \to \cdot$ / $C \to \cdot$.
4 counts the four $\epsilon$-states $I_0, I_2, I_3, I_6$ but misses $I_9$, where $B \to b\cdot$ clashes with shifting another $b$.
Exactly $I_0, I_2, I_3, I_6, I_9$ have a complete item next to a shift on a terminal.

cse-2026-2-cs-31.shortcut: Each of $A \to aA \mid \epsilon$ and $C \to cC \mid \epsilon$ gives two conflicting states (the one where the non-terminal is first expected, and the one after shifting its terminal, which re-closes over the $\epsilon$-item): $2 + 2 = 4$. $B \to bB \mid b$ gives one more (after shifting $b$, both $B \to b\cdot$ and $B \to \cdot b\ldots$ are present): $4 + 1 = 5$.

Using FOLLOW sets (that is SLR(1)); in LR(0) a reduce item reduces on every terminal, so FOLLOW does not remove anything.
Forgetting that the closure in $I_3$ and $I_6$ again adds the $\epsilon$-item $A \to \cdot$ / $C \to \cdot$.

cse-2026-2-cs-32.approach: Write the shortest derivation of Union and then check which rules it really uses: augment each premise once, then chain with transitivity. Reflexivity is never needed, while neither augmentation nor transitivity can be dropped.
cse-2026-2-cs-32.given: Premises $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$; goal $X \to YZ$.

steps.title: Augment X → Y with X
steps.body:
Augmentation with $Z := X$ on $X \to Y$ gives $XX \to XY$. Since $XX = X$ (attribute sets), this is

$$X \to XY.$$

steps.title: Augment X → Z with Y
steps.body:
Augmentation with $Y$ on $X \to Z$ gives

$$XY \to YZ.$$

steps.title: Chain them with transitivity
steps.body:
From $X \to XY$ and $XY \to YZ$, transitivity gives

$$X \to YZ.$$

The proof used **augmentation** (twice) and **transitivity** (once) — no reflexivity. So augmentation + transitivity is **sufficient**.

steps.title: Both rules are necessary
steps.body:
Take $F = \{A \to B,\ A \to C\}$ (single attributes) and goal $A \to BC$.

- **Without transitivity**: reflexivity and augmentation each take a *single* premise, so every derived FD comes from just one of $A \to B$, $A \to C$, or from a trivial FD. From $A \to B$ alone, augmentation only gives $AW \to BW$, so a left side of exactly $A$ yields only $A \to B$ or $A \to AB$ — never $C$ on the right. Two premises can never be combined, so $A \to BC$ is unreachable.
- **Without augmentation**: reflexivity gives only trivial FDs and transitivity only chains existing ones, so every right side reachable from $A$ is $B$, $C$ or a subset of $A$ — again never $BC$.

So both are needed and reflexivity is not: the answer is option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Sufficient but not *necessary*: the proof above never uses reflexivity, so this set is not minimal.
Without transitivity the two premises can never be combined — both rules act on one FD at a time.
Transitivity alone only chains existing FDs; no right side ever grows to $YZ$.
$X\to Y \Rightarrow X \to XY$; $X \to Z \Rightarrow XY \to YZ$; transitivity gives $X \to YZ$. Each of the two rules is indispensable.

cse-2026-2-cs-32.shortcut: Union needs (1) a rule that combines two FDs — only transitivity takes two premises — and (2) a rule that enlarges a right-hand side — only augmentation does. Reflexivity just produces trivial FDs, which this proof does not need.
pitfalls: Answering "all three" because Armstrong's axioms are usually quoted together — the question asks for a set that is both *necessary* and sufficient.
Thinking reflexivity is needed to get $X \to X$; augmenting $X \to Y$ with $X$ already gives $X \to XY$ directly.
cse-2026-2-cs-32.verification: Semantic check: if two tuples agree on $X$ they agree on $Y$ and on $Z$, hence on $YZ$ — so Union is sound, and the 3-line derivation above is the textbook proof (Silberschatz, Union rule).

cse-2026-2-cs-33.approach: The generator $1001$ has degree 3, so append three 0s and divide modulo 2 (XOR long division); the 3-bit remainder is the CRC. Because $x^3 + 1$ means $x^3 \equiv 1$, the remainder is also just the XOR of the 3-bit chunks — a fast cross-check.

steps.title: Append r = 3 zeros
steps.body:
The degree of $G$ is $r = 3$, so the dividend is $D \cdot x^3$:

$$110001011\,000 \quad (12 \text{ bits}).$$

steps.title: Read the remainder
steps.body: The remainder is $100$, so the transmitted frame is $110001011\,\mathbf{100}$. Option **(D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $011$ is not what the division leaves: the frame $110001011\,011$ gives chunk-XOR $110 \oplus 001 \oplus 011 \oplus 011 = 111 \neq 000$, so the receiver would flag an error.
$101$ does not come out of the division: $110 \oplus 001 \oplus 011 \oplus 101 = 001 \neq 000$, so $110001011\,101$ is not a multiple of $1001$.
$000$ would mean $D\cdot x^3$ is already a multiple of $G$; the division leaves $100$.

cse-2026-2-cs-33.shortcut: $G = x^3 + 1$ means $x^3 \equiv 1 \pmod G$, so bits three places apart fold onto each other. Split $110001011000$ into 3-bit chunks from the right and XOR them: $110 \oplus 001 \oplus 011 \oplus 000 = 111 \oplus 011 = 100$.
pitfalls: Forgetting to append $r = 3$ zeros before dividing.
Appending 4 zeros (the generator *length*) instead of 3 (its degree).
Using ordinary subtraction with borrows instead of XOR.
cse-2026-2-cs-33.verification: The frame $110001011100$ must divide exactly by $1001$: chunk-XOR $110 \oplus 001 \oplus 011 \oplus 100 = 000$. ✓

cse-2026-2-cs-34.approach: Use expanding opcodes: give the format with the most operand bits the shortest opcode, and let each unused opcode pattern act as a prefix for the next, longer opcode. Equivalently, count how much of the $2^{16}$ encoding space each instruction uses — a one-line computation.
cse-2026-2-cs-34.given:
16-bit instructions; 16 registers $\Rightarrow$ $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits per register field.

| type | operands | operand bits | opcode bits |
|---|---|---|---|
| M | 2 reg + 6-bit imm | $4+4+6 = 14$ | $16-14 = 2$ |
| R | 3 reg | $4 \times 3 = 12$ | $16-12 = 4$ |
| C | 1 reg + 6-bit offset | $4+6 = 10$ | $16-10 = 6$ |

steps.title: M-type: 2-bit opcodes
steps.body: A 2-bit opcode has $2^2 = 4$ patterns. M uses $2$ (say $00$, $01$), leaving $4 - 2 = 2$ free patterns ($10$, $11$) to expand.

steps.title: R-type: 4-bit opcodes
steps.body: Each free 2-bit prefix extends by $4 - 2 = 2$ more bits: $2 \times 2^2 = 8$ four-bit patterns ($10xx$, $11xx$). R uses $7$, leaving $8 - 7 = 1$ free pattern (say $1111$).

scene.caption: 8 four-bit patterns 10xx, 11xx: 7 for R, 1111 left over.

steps.title: C-type: 6-bit opcodes
steps.body: The one free 4-bit prefix extends by $6 - 4 = 2$ bits: $1 \times 2^2 = 4$ patterns ($1111\,00$ … $1111\,11$). So at most **4** C-type opcodes — option **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: 8 is the number of 4-bit patterns available to R *before* R takes 7 of them; it forgets to subtract R's opcodes (or treats C's opcode as 5 bits).
One free 4-bit prefix $\times\ 2^2$ extensions $= 4$; the encoding-space count gives $4096/1024 = 4$ too.
64 $= 2^6$ is every 6-bit pattern, ignoring that M and R already consume most of the opcode space.
16 would follow from treating the leftover as 2 free 4-bit prefixes or from $2^4$; with 7 R-opcodes only one 4-bit prefix remains.

pitfalls: Using 16 bits per register (the register *count*) instead of $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits.
Forgetting that every leftover opcode pattern multiplies by $2^{\Delta}$ when the opcode grows by $\Delta$ bits.

cse-2026-2-cs-35.approach: Live-variable analysis is a backward data-flow problem: $OUT[B] = \bigcup_{S \in succ(B)} IN[S]$ and $IN[B] = use[B] \cup (OUT[B] - def[B])$. Iterate from the exit (B4) backwards until nothing changes; the loop B1 → B3 → B1 needs a second pass.

steps.title: B4 and B2 (no loop involved)
steps.body:
B4 flows to EXIT, and nothing is used after it: $OUT[B4] = \emptyset$, so $IN[B4] = \{d, e\} \cup (\emptyset - \{g\}) = \{d, e\}$.

B2's only successor is B4: $OUT[B2] = \{d, e\}$, so $IN[B2] = \{a, e\} \cup (\{d, e\} - \{d\}) = \{a, e\}$.

steps.title: Pass 1 over the loop
steps.body:
Start with $IN[B1] = \emptyset$ (initial value).

- $OUT[B3] = IN[B1] = \emptyset$, so $IN[B3] = \{a, f\} \cup (\emptyset - \{e\}) = \{a, f\}$.
- $OUT[B1] = IN[B2] \cup IN[B3] = \{a, e\} \cup \{a, f\} = \{a, e, f\}$.
- $IN[B1] = \{b, c\} \cup (\{a, e, f\} - \{a\}) = \{b, c, e, f\}$.

$IN[B1]$ changed, so B3 must be recomputed.

steps.title: Pass 2: propagate around the back edge
steps.body:
- $OUT[B3] = IN[B1] = \{b, c, e, f\}$, so $IN[B3] = \{a, f\} \cup (\{b, c, e, f\} - \{e\}) = \{a, b, c, f\}$.
- $OUT[B1] = \{a, e\} \cup \{a, b, c, f\} = \{a, b, c, e, f\}$.
- $IN[B1] = \{b, c\} \cup (\{a, b, c, e, f\} - \{a\}) = \{b, c, e, f\}$ — unchanged.

A third pass changes nothing, so this is the fixed point.

steps.title: Read the OUT column
steps.body:
$$OUT[B1] = \{a,b,c,e,f\},\ OUT[B2] = \{d,e\},\ OUT[B3] = \{b,c,e,f\},\ OUT[B4] = \emptyset.$$

This is option **(A)**. Note $e$ is live at the exit of B3 even though B3 assigns $e$: the new value flows B3 → B1 → B2, and B1 does not redefine $e$.

$OUT[B1] = \emptyset$ ignores that B2 and B3 read $a$, $e$, $f$ right after B1; and $\{a, c, f\}$ at B3's exit drops $b$, $e$ and wrongly keeps $a$, which B1 overwrites before any read.
Misses $b$ at B3's exit: B3 → B1 and B1 reads $b$ before anything writes it.
$OUT[B1]$ cannot be empty, and $f$ is not live after B2 (only B4 follows, which uses $d$, $e$); $a$ is dead at B3's exit because B1 redefines it.

cse-2026-2-cs-36.approach: Ask how each index finds a key that has **no** entry of its own. A sparse index works only if the file is sorted on the key and the index preserves that order, so you can jump to the nearest smaller entry and scan forward. A B$^+$ tree preserves order (so it may be sparse); a hash index scatters keys, so every key needs its own entry.

steps.title: S1: a hash index must be dense
steps.body: A hash index stores each entry in the bucket $h(\text{key})$. To find key $k$ you look only in bucket $h(k)$. If $k$ had no entry, there is no "nearest smaller key" to fall back on — hashing destroys the order, and neighbouring keys land in unrelated buckets. So every search-key value must have its own entry: a hash index is **always dense**. S1 is **true**.

steps.title: S2: a B+ tree index can be sparse
steps.body: If the data file is sorted on the search key (a clustering index), the B$^+$ tree can store just one entry per data block (e.g. the first key in the block). To find $k$, descend to the largest entry $\le k$, go to that block and scan it. That is a sparse index. (Inside every B$^+$ tree the non-leaf levels are a sparse index on the leaf level anyway.) S2 is **true**.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both statements are true — option **(A)**.

answer.value: Both S1 and S2 are true — option **(A)**

optionAnalysis.reason: Hashing loses order, so it needs an entry per key; an order-preserving B$^+$ tree over a sorted file can index one key per block.
Both statements hold; "false" for S2 confuses "can be sparse" with "must be sparse".
S2 is true: a clustering B$^+$ tree index on a sorted file may be sparse.
S1 is true: a hash index cannot locate a key that has no entry, so it cannot be sparse.

cse-2026-2-cs-36.shortcut: Sparse needs order. B$^+$ tree = ordered → *can* be sparse; hash = unordered → *must* be dense.

Thinking a hash index could be sparse because buckets hold several keys — a bucket still needs an entry for each key it holds.
cse-2026-2-cs-36.verification: Textbook check (Silberschatz, *Database System Concepts*, indexing chapter): hash indices are only secondary (hence dense) indices, while a B$^+$-tree on a sequentially ordered file may be sparse.

cse-2026-2-cs-38.approach: Ask whether a single stack can check the constraint while reading $a^i b^j c^k d^\ell$ left to right. Constraints that are one *signed counter* ($i+k = j+\ell$, $i+j = k+\ell$) or *nested* matches ($i=\ell$ around $j=k$) are context-free; two *crossing* equalities ($i=k$, $j=\ell$) are not.

steps.title: A: i + k = j + ℓ is context-free
steps.body: Rewrite as $i - j + k - \ell = 0$: a running counter that goes $+1$ on $a$, $-1$ on $b$, $+1$ on $c$, $-1$ on $d$ must end at $0$. A PDA keeps the counter on its stack with a sign: symbol $X$ for a positive value, $Y$ for a negative one. On a $+1$ symbol pop $Y$ if the top is $Y$, else push $X$; on a $-1$ symbol pop $X$ if the top is $X$, else push $Y$. Its finite control also checks the order $a^*b^*c^*d^*$. Accept when the stack is empty. **CFL.**

steps.title: D: i + j = k + ℓ is context-free
steps.body:
Push one symbol per $a$ and per $b$, pop one per $c$ and per $d$; accept on an empty stack. A grammar also works:

$$S \to aSd \mid T \mid V,\quad T \to aTc \mid U,\quad V \to bVd \mid U,\quad U \to bUc \mid \epsilon.$$

($S$ matches $a$ with $d$; then the leftover $a$'s pair with $c$'s, or the leftover $d$'s with $b$'s; finally $b$'s pair with $c$'s.) **CFL.**

steps.title: C: i = ℓ and j = k is context-free
steps.body:
The language is $\{a^i b^j c^j d^i\}$: the $b$–$c$ match sits **inside** the $a$–$d$ match (nested, like brackets):

$$S \to aSd \mid T,\qquad T \to bTc \mid \epsilon.$$

**CFL.**

steps.title: B: i = k and j = ℓ is not context-free
steps.body:
The language is $\{a^i b^j c^i d^j\}$: the $a$–$c$ and $b$–$d$ matches **cross**. Pumping lemma: take $z = a^p b^p c^p d^p$ with $p$ the pumping length. Any split $z = uvwxy$ with $\lvert vwx \rvert \le p$ and $\lvert vx \rvert \ge 1$ has $vwx$ inside at most two adjacent blocks. Pumping to $uv^2wx^2y$ then changes the count of $a$ without $c$ (or $c$ without $a$), or $b$ without $d$, or puts letters out of order. So $uv^2wx^2y \notin L$: **not a CFL.**

Answer: **(A), (C), (D)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $i - j + k - \ell = 0$ is one signed counter, which a PDA keeps on its stack.
$a^i b^j c^i d^j$ has crossing dependencies; the pumping lemma with $a^p b^p c^p d^p$ breaks it.
$a^i b^j c^j d^i$ is nested: $S \to aSd \mid T$, $T \to bTc \mid \epsilon$.
Push for $a, b$; pop for $c, d$ — one counter. Grammar $S \to aSd \mid T \mid V$, $T \to aTc \mid U$, $V \to bVd \mid U$, $U \to bUc \mid \epsilon$.

cse-2026-2-cs-38.shortcut: Draw arcs between the blocks each constraint links. Equalities of sums (A, D) are a single counter — CFL. Arcs that nest (C: $a$–$d$ outside $b$–$c$) — CFL. Arcs that cross (B: $a$–$c$ and $b$–$d$) — not CFL.
pitfalls: Rejecting (A) because $a$ and $c$ both "add" and are not adjacent — a signed counter does not care where the $+1$ and $-1$ symbols are.
Treating the question as single-answer: it is multiple-select (three constraints work).
cse-2026-2-cs-38.verification: Test the (D) grammar on both cases. $i > \ell$: $a^2cd$ ($2+0 = 1+1$): $S \Rightarrow aSd \Rightarrow aTd \Rightarrow aaTcd \Rightarrow aaUcd \Rightarrow aacd$ ✓. $i < \ell$: $abd^2$ ($1+1 = 0+2$): $S \Rightarrow aSd \Rightarrow aVd \Rightarrow abVdd \Rightarrow abUdd \Rightarrow abdd$ ✓. And $a^1b^1c^1d^1$ fits (A), (C), (D) but also (B) — so (B) is excluded by the pumping argument, not by a single string.

cse-2026-2-cs-39.approach: Use one structural fact: a leaf $L$ has no right subtree, so its inorder successor is an **ancestor**, and no key of the tree lies strictly between $Val(L)$ and $Val(Suc(L))$. Hence each new key $k_i$ lands as the right child of its own leaf $L_i$. Every option follows from this; a small example and a one-node tree settle the rest.

steps.title: Where does each new key go?
steps.body:
$L_i$ is a leaf and $Suc(L_i)$ is the next key in sorted (inorder) order, so no key of the tree lies in the open interval $(Val(L_i), Val(Suc(L_i)))$. Searching for $k_i$ therefore compares exactly like searching for $Val(L_i)$ at every ancestor and ends at $L_i$; since $k_i > Val(L_i)$ it becomes the **right child of $L_i$**.

Example: leaves $20, 40, 60, 80$ with successors $30, 50, 70$ and NULL (80 is the maximum). So $K = (25, 45, 65)$, for instance.

scene.caption: Leaves 20, 40, 60 have successors 30, 50, 70; leaf 80 has none.

steps.title: A: no duplicates
steps.body: Different leaves are different keys, and the intervals $(Val(L_i), Val(Suc(L_i)))$ are gaps between **consecutive** keys in sorted order, so they are pairwise disjoint. One number cannot lie in two disjoint intervals: $K$ has **no duplicates**. (A) true.

steps.title: C: height grows by at most one
steps.body:
Each $k_i$ hangs directly below a leaf, at depth $\text{depth}(L_i) + 1 \le h + 1$. Inserting the other keys does not change this, because they lie in other gaps and so never sit on $k_i$'s search path between $L_i$ and $Suc(L_i)$. The new height is at most $h + 1$. (C) true.

In the example: insert 25, 45, 65 → each becomes a right child of 20, 40, 60, and the height goes from 2 to 3.

scene.caption: K = 25, 45, 65 become right children of 20, 40, 60: height 2 → 3.

steps.title: B and D are false
steps.body:
- (B): take a BST with a single node. It is a leaf ($n = 1 > 0$) and the maximum, so $Suc = NULL$ and $K$ is **empty**. (A right-going chain $10 \to 20 \to 30$ works too: its only leaf, 30, is the maximum.) (B) false.
- (D): the number of new keys is at most the number of leaves. In the example the tree grows from $7$ to $7 + 3 = 10$ nodes, not $14$. In general a tree with $N \ge 2$ nodes has fewer than $N$ leaves, and for $N = 1$ nothing is added, so the count never doubles. (D) false.

Answer: **(A), (C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: The intervals between consecutive keys are disjoint, so the $k_i$ are distinct.
A one-node tree (or any tree whose only leaf is the maximum) has no leaf with a successor, so $K$ is empty.
Every $k_i$ becomes the right child of a leaf, so depth grows by at most 1.
At most one key per leaf is added; e.g. 7 nodes become 10, not 14.

cse-2026-2-cs-39.shortcut: Remember "a leaf's successor is an ancestor" — then $k_i$ must be the leaf's right child. Disjoint gaps ⇒ (A); one level below leaves ⇒ (C); a single-node tree kills (B); counting leaves kills (D).
pitfalls: Assuming every BST has a leaf with a successor — the maximum key can be the only leaf.
Worrying that inserting $k_1$ first could change where $k_2$ goes — it cannot, because they lie in different gaps between consecutive keys.
cse-2026-2-cs-39.verification: Inorder after insertion in the example: $20, 25, 30, 40, 45, 50, 60, 65, 70, 80$ — still sorted, and each new key sits right after its leaf, as derived.

cse-2026-2-cs-40.approach: The output is (all of $S$ popped) followed by (all of $Q$ dequeued). Elements arrive in increasing order, so the $S$-part comes out **decreasing** and the $Q$-part **increasing**. Just find every way to cut $4\,3\,1\,2\,5$ into a decreasing prefix and an increasing suffix.
cse-2026-2-cs-40.given: Arrivals $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$; output $4\,3\,1\,2\,5$ = pops of $S$, then dequeues of $Q$.

steps.title: Shape of any output
steps.body: Elements are pushed/enqueued in increasing order $1 < 2 < \dots < 5$. Popping a stack returns them in reverse, so the $S$-part is **strictly decreasing**; dequeuing returns them in order, so the $Q$-part is **strictly increasing**. Conversely, any such split is achievable: send the prefix elements to $S$ and the rest to $Q$.

steps.title: Option A: S = {1, 3, 4}, Q = {2, 5}
steps.body: Push $1$, enqueue $2$, push $3$, push $4$, enqueue $5$. $S$ (bottom → top) $= 1, 3, 4$ pops as $4, 3, 1$; $Q = 2, 5$ dequeues as $2, 5$. Output $4\,3\,1\,2\,5$ ✓.

steps.title: Options C and D fail
steps.body:
- (C) $S = \{4, 5\}$ pops $5, 4$ first: output starts $5\,4 \ldots$ ✗.
- (D) $S = \{1, 2, 3\}$ pops $3, 2, 1$, then $Q$ gives $4, 5$: output $3\,2\,1\,4\,5$ ✗.

Answer: **(A), (B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: The stack holds $4, 5$, so the first element out is $5$, not $4$.
Gives $3\,2\,1\,4\,5$; it reads the output as if $S$ came out in arrival order.

cse-2026-2-cs-40.shortcut: Decreasing prefix + increasing suffix: $4\,3\,|\,1\,2\,5$ and $4\,3\,1\,|\,2\,5$ are the only cuts — the options listing $S=\{3,4\}$ or $S=\{1,3,4\}$ are (B) and (A).
pitfalls: Forgetting that element $1$ can go either way: it is the last pop of $S$ in (A) and the first dequeue of $Q$ in (B).
Treating the question as single-answer — two assignments are valid.
cse-2026-2-cs-40.verification: Simulate both valid options element by element (done in steps 3–4); both reproduce $4\,3\,1\,2\,5$ exactly, and the cut table shows no third split exists.

cse-2026-2-cs-41.approach: Find the invariants: (1) the second process to enter the $A$-protected section prints $\texttt{\textdollar }$ right after its own $\texttt{*}$, while still holding $A$, so every output starts $\texttt{**\textdollar }$; (2) $\texttt{\#}$ needs $B$, which first becomes 1 at that $\texttt{\textdollar }$. After that the third $\texttt{*}$ can fall anywhere among the three $\texttt{\#}$. One concrete schedule per pattern proves it possible.
cse-2026-2-cs-41.given:
A = 1 (mutex), B = 0, X = 0. Each of P1, P2, P3 runs, one atomic line at a time:

1. `Wait(A);` `Print(*);` `X = X+1;`
2. if X == 2: Print($\texttt{\textdollar }$); `Signal(B);`
3. `Signal(A);`
4. `Wait(B);` `Print(#);` `Signal(B);`

steps.title: Every output begins with two stars and the dollar
steps.body: $A$ is a mutex around Print(*), $X = X+1$ and the If. The process that makes $X = 2$ is the **second** one in; it prints $\texttt{\textdollar }$ before its Signal(A), so a third process cannot print $\texttt{*}$ in between. Before that no $\texttt{\#}$ is possible: $B = 0$, and the first Signal(B) is the one inside the If. So the output begins $\texttt{**\textdollar }$, and the remaining four symbols are one $\texttt{*}$ and three $\texttt{\#}$.

scene.caption: P2 prints the dollar while it still holds A.

steps.title: B is a turnstile, so all three hashes appear
steps.body: Each process does Wait(B); Print(#); Signal(B): it takes the single token and passes it on. So every process eventually prints $\texttt{\#}$. Total output: three $\texttt{*}$, one $\texttt{\textdollar }$, three $\texttt{\#}$ — 7 symbols, as in every option.

steps.title: Pattern (C) is possible
steps.body: The table traces one schedule: P1 and P2 print $\texttt{\#}$ before P3 even starts; then P3 prints $\texttt{*}$ and its own $\texttt{\#}$. Output $\texttt{**\textdollar \#\#*\#}$ ✓.

steps.title: Patterns (A) and (B) are possible
Pattern (D) is impossible
steps.body:
$\texttt{***\textdollar \#\#\#}$ needs a third $\texttt{*}$ before $\texttt{\textdollar }$, i.e. a third process inside the $A$-section while the second one has not yet printed $\texttt{\textdollar }$. The second one still holds $A$ then, so this cannot happen. (D) is false.

Answer: **(A), (B), (C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: P3 enters right after P2's Signal(A), before anyone passes Wait(B).
P1 prints $\texttt{\#}$ first, then P3 prints $\texttt{*}$, then the remaining two $\texttt{\#}$.
P1 and P2 both print $\texttt{\#}$ before P3 runs at all (traced in the table).
The $\texttt{\textdollar }$ is printed by the second process inside the mutex right after its $\texttt{*}$, so only two $\texttt{*}$ can precede it.

cse-2026-2-cs-41.shortcut: "$\texttt{\textdollar }$ comes right after the 2nd $\texttt{*}$" kills (D) at once; every other position of the leftover $\texttt{*}$ among the $\texttt{\#}$s is reachable.
pitfalls: Thinking $\texttt{\#}$ can appear only after all three $\texttt{*}$ — the third process may still be waiting for $A$ (or not have started).
Forgetting that Signal(B) after each $\texttt{\#}$ lets the next waiter through, so all three $\texttt{\#}$ do appear.
cse-2026-2-cs-41.verification: Counting check: a valid pattern has 3 $\texttt{*}$, 1 $\texttt{\textdollar }$, 3 $\texttt{\#}$ and starts with $\texttt{**\textdollar }$. (A), (B), (C) satisfy this and each has an explicit schedule; (D) violates the prefix.

cse-2026-2-cs-42.approach: Split each address into tag / line / offset. Words in the same block share a line fill; words with the same line but different tags evict each other. Then one round of P, Q, R, S shows the steady pattern for all ten rounds.
cse-2026-2-cs-42.given:
Cache $4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}$ B, block $16 = 2^4$ B ⇒ $2^{12}/2^4 = 2^8 = 256$ lines. Memory $16\text{ MB} = 2^{24}$ B ⇒ 24-bit addresses.

$$\underbrace{24}_{\text{address}} = \underbrace{12}_{\text{tag}} + \underbrace{8}_{\text{line}} + \underbrace{4}_{\text{offset}}$$

steps.title: Split the four addresses
steps.body:
With 6 hex digits: tag = first 3, line = next 2, offset = last 1.

| word | address | tag | line | offset |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 0x845B32 | 845 | B3 | 2 |
| Q | 0x845B26 | 845 | B2 | 6 |
| R | 0x845B36 | 845 | B3 | 6 |
| S | 0x846B32 | **846** | B3 | 2 |

P and R are in the **same block** (tag 845, line B3). S maps to the same line B3 with a different tag. Q is alone in line B2.

steps.title: Round 1
steps.body:
- P: line B3 empty → **miss**, load block 845|B3.
- Q: line B2 empty → **miss**, load 845|B2.
- R: line B3 holds tag 845 → **hit** (same block as P).
- S: line B3 holds 845, needs 846 → **miss**, evicts P/R's block.

steps.title: Rounds 2–10 repeat one pattern
steps.body:
At the start of each later round line B3 holds S's block (846) and line B2 holds Q's block.

- P: B3 has 846 → **miss**, reload 845.
- Q: B2 still has 845 → **hit**.
- R: B3 now has 845 → **hit**.
- S: B3 has 845 → **miss**, reload 846.

So P misses all 10 times, R hits all 10 times, Q misses once and hits 9 times, S misses all 10 times.

steps.title: Judge the statements
steps.body:
- (A) every access to P misses — **true**.
- (B) every access to R hits — **true** (P always brings R's block in just before R).
- (C) every access to Q misses — false (only the first).
- (D) S hits after the first access — false (S always misses; P evicts it every round).

Answer: **(A), (B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: P and S fight over line B3; S evicts P's block every round, so P always misses.
R is in the same 16-byte block as P (0x845B30–0x845B3F), and P loads it immediately before R in every round.
Q has line B2 to itself: one compulsory miss, then 9 hits.
P's miss reloads tag 845 into line B3 before every S, so S misses all 10 times.

cse-2026-2-cs-42.shortcut: Hex digits map straight onto the split (12 + 8 + 4 bits = 3 + 2 + 1 hex digits). P, R, S share line B3; P and R share the block; S has another tag → P and S always miss, R always hits, Q misses once.
pitfalls: Calling R a miss because S just evicted the line — P's access in between reloads the block that also contains R.
Using word addressing tricks: here 1 word = 1 byte, so the offset is simply the last hex digit.

cse-2026-2-cs-43.approach: Count the block numbers to be stored (one per disk block, i.e. the whole disk free) and divide by how many block numbers fit in one list block after reserving the 4-byte next pointer; round **up**.
cse-2026-2-cs-43.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Disk | $16\text{ GB} = 2^{34}$ B |
| Block | $2\text{ KB} = 2^{11}$ B |
| Block number / pointer | 32 bits = 4 B |

steps.title: Number of disk blocks
steps.body:
Every block number on the disk may have to be recorded (the worst case — the whole disk free):

$$\frac{2^{34}}{2^{11}} = 2^{23} = 8\,388\,608 \text{ block numbers}$$

steps.title: Block numbers per list block
steps.body:
A 2 KB block holds $\frac{2^{11}}{4} = 2^{9} = 512$ four-byte entries. One entry is the pointer to the next block of the list, so each list block stores

$$512 - 1 = 511 \text{ free block numbers}$$

steps.title: Blocks needed (round up)
steps.body:
$$\left\lceil \frac{8\,388\,608}{511} \right\rceil$$

$511 \times 16\,416 = 8\,388\,576$, which leaves $8\,388\,608 - 8\,388\,576 = 32$ block numbers, so one more block is needed:

$$16\,416 + 1 = 16\,417$$

pitfalls: Forgetting the next-pointer: $2^{23}/512 = 16384$.
Rounding down to 16416 — the last 32 block numbers still need a block.
Using the bitmap approach ($2^{23}$ bits $= 2^{20}$ B $= 512$ blocks) — the question fixes the linked-list approach.

cse-2026-2-cs-44.approach: TLB reach ÷ page size gives the number of entries; each entry is PID + virtual page number + frame number + control bits. Multiply.
cse-2026-2-cs-44.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| TLB reach | $1\text{ MB} = 2^{20}$ B |
| Page | $4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}$ B |
| VA space | $64\text{ GB} = 2^{36}$ B |
| PA space | $1\text{ GB} = 2^{30}$ B |
| Extra fields | PID 4 bits, control 2 bits |

steps.title: Number of TLB entries
steps.body:
Each entry maps one page, so

$$\text{entries} = \frac{\text{reach}}{\text{page size}} = \frac{2^{20}}{2^{12}} = 2^{8} = 256$$

steps.title: Page and frame number widths
steps.body:
Offset = $\log_2 2^{12} = 12$ bits.

- Page number: $36 - 12 = 24$ bits (VA is $2^{36}$).
- Frame number: $30 - 12 = 18$ bits (PA is $2^{30}$).

steps.title: Entry size and TLB size
steps.body:
$$4 + 24 + 18 + 2 = 48 \text{ bits} = 6 \text{ bytes}$$

$$\text{TLB size} = 256 \times 6 = 1536 \text{ bytes}$$

pitfalls: Using the virtual address space for the number of entries — the entry count comes from the reach.
Using full addresses (36 or 30 bits) instead of page/frame numbers (offset bits are not stored).
Leaving the answer in bits ($256 \times 48 = 12288$).
cse-2026-2-cs-44.verification: Reach check: $256$ entries $\times 4$ KB $= 1024$ KB $= 1$ MB ✓. Bit total: $256 \times 48 = 12288$ bits $= 1536$ B ✓.

cse-2026-2-cs-45.approach: Simulate best fit: each process takes the **smallest hole that is large enough**; the leftover of that hole stays as a smaller hole (an exact fit leaves no hole). Then count holes below 8 KB.
cse-2026-2-cs-45.given: Holes (KB): $20, 4, 25, 18, 7, 9, 15, 12$ (none adjacent, so no coalescing). P1 = 16 KB, then P2 = 9 KB.

steps.title: P1 (16 KB) takes the 18 KB hole
steps.body:
Holes $\ge 16$: $20, 25, 18$. The smallest is $18$.

Leftover: $18 - 16 = 2$ KB hole.

steps.title: P2 (9 KB) takes the 9 KB hole
steps.body:
Current holes: $20, 4, 25, 2, 7, 9, 15, 12$. Holes $\ge 9$: $20, 25, 9, 15, 12$. The smallest is $9$ — an exact fit.

Leftover: $9 - 9 = 0$, so that hole disappears.

steps.title: Count holes smaller than 8 KB
steps.body:
Remaining holes: $20, 4, 25, 2, 7, 15, 12$.

Below 8 KB: $4, 2, 7$ → **3** holes.

cse-2026-2-cs-45.shortcut: Before: only 4 and 7 are below 8 KB. P1 creates a 2 KB sliver (18 − 16); P2 fits exactly (no sliver). $2 + 1 = 3$.
pitfalls: Counting the 0 KB remainder of the 9 KB hole as a hole (gives 4).
Using first fit (P1 → 20, leaving 4; P2 → 25 or the 9 depending on order) — that changes the count.
Allocating P2 before P1 — they arrive in the order P1, P2.

cse-2026-2-cs-46.approach: In a direct-mapped cache the block number is the **index** field of the address. Find where the bit pattern of 176 sits in the address (that fixes the offset width), then widen the index upward over zero bits as far as possible: cache size $= 2^{\text{index}+\text{offset}}$.
cse-2026-2-cs-46.given: Physical address: 20 bits ($1\text{ MB} = 2^{20}$, byte-addressable). Address $\text{0xA2C28}$ maps to cache block $176$.

steps.title: Write the address and 176 in binary
steps.body:
$\text{0xA2C28} = 1010\;0010\;1100\;0010\;1000$ (bits 19…0).

$176 = 128 + 32 + 16 = 10110000_2$ (8 bits).

With block size $2^b$ and $2^n$ cache blocks, block number $= \lfloor A / 2^b \rfloor \bmod 2^n$ = bits $b+n-1 \ldots b$ of the address. So the index field must read $0\ldots0\,10110000$.

steps.title: Locate 10110000 → offset is 6 bits
steps.body:
The pattern $10110000$ appears only once in the address: bits $13 \ldots 6$ ($1,0,1,1,0,0,0,0$). Hence the offset is bits $5\ldots0$: $b = 6$, block size $2^6 = 64$ B.

(No other alignment works: the only `1011` in the address is at bits 13…10.)

steps.title: Widen the index as far as possible
steps.body:
Extra index bits above bit 13 are allowed only while they are $0$ (otherwise the block number would exceed 176). Bits 14, 15, 16 are $0$; bit 17 is $1$.

So the index can be at most bits $16\ldots6$: $n = 11$ bits ($00010110000_2 = 176$ ✓), tag = bits 19…17.

cse-2026-2-cs-46.shortcut: Spot `1011 0000` in `0xA2C28` = `1010 0010 1100 0010 1000`: it sits right above the low 6 bits; leading zeros above it run up to bit 16 → $11 + 6 = 17$ bits → $2^{17}$ B $= 128$ KB.
pitfalls: Assuming the index is exactly 8 bits (gives $2^{14}$ B = 16 KB) — leading zero bits can also belong to the index.
Extending the index over bit 17 (a 1) — the block number would become $2048 + 176$.
Treating 176 as hexadecimal; it is $176_{10}$.

cse-2026-2-cs-47.approach: Compare average time per instruction: non-pipelined $= \text{CPI} \times T_{clk} = 5/1.6$ ns; pipelined $= (1 + \text{stall cycles per instruction}) / 1.2$ ns. Speed-up is their ratio.
cse-2026-2-cs-47.given:
| Design | Clock | CPI |
|---|---|---|
| Non-pipelined | 1.6 GHz | 5 |
| Pipelined | 1.2 GHz | $1 + 0.3 \times 2$ |

steps.title: Pipelined CPI and time per instruction
steps.body:
Ideal CPI is 1; 30% of instructions add 2 stall cycles:

$$\text{CPI}_p = 1 + 0.3 \times 2 = 1.6$$

$$T_p = \frac{1.6}{1.2 \times 10^{9}} \text{ s} = 1.3\overline{3} \text{ ns}$$

pitfalls: Ignoring the clock change: $5/1.6 = 3.125$ (CPI ratio only).
Ignoring the stalls: $3.125/(1/1.2) = 3.75$.
cse-2026-2-cs-47.verification: For $10^9$ instructions: non-pipelined $5 \times 10^9$ cycles at 1.6 GHz $= 3.125$ s; pipelined $1.6 \times 10^9$ cycles at 1.2 GHz $= 1.333$ s; $3.125 / 1.333 = 2.34$ ✓.

cse-2026-2-cs-48.approach: Slow start begins at cwnd = 1 MSS and doubles every round (RTT) until cwnd reaches ssthresh; count the transmission rounds until cwnd = ssthresh. The 48 KB receiver window never limits.
cse-2026-2-cs-48.given: MSS = 2 KB, ssthresh = 16 KB = 8 MSS, rwnd = 48 KB (constant), no timeouts / duplicate ACKs.

steps.title: Express everything in MSS
steps.body: Initial cwnd $= 1$ MSS $= 2$ KB; $\text{ssthresh} = 16/2 = 8$ MSS; rwnd $= 48/2 = 24$ MSS, which is larger than anything slow start reaches here, so it plays no role.

steps.title: Double each round
steps.body:
| Round | cwnd (MSS) | cwnd (KB) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 4 | 8 |
| 4 | 8 | 16 |

Each ACKed segment adds 1 MSS, so cwnd doubles per round.

steps.title: Round 4 reaches ssthresh
steps.body:
In round 4 cwnd $= 8$ MSS $= 16$ KB $=$ ssthresh, so TCP leaves slow start and enters **congestion avoidance** (growth becomes +1 MSS per RTT: 18 KB in round 5).

Rounds required: $1, 2, 4, 8$ MSS → **4**.

scene.caption: Round 5 grows linearly (+1 MSS) — congestion avoidance

pitfalls: Starting cwnd at 2 KB but counting doublings only ($\log_2 8 = 3$) — the first round (cwnd = 1 MSS) is also a round of transmission.
Using the receiver window 48 KB as the threshold.
Working in KB without converting via MSS and starting cwnd at 1 KB.
cse-2026-2-cs-48.verification: Segments sent per round: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15$; the window used in round 4 is $8 \times 2 = 16$ KB = ssthresh, and from round 5 the window grows linearly.

cse-2026-2-cs-49.approach: Write the MUX output as a sum over the four select values: $Y = \bar S_1 \bar S_0 D_0 + \bar S_1 S_0 \cdot 0 + S_1 \bar S_0 \cdot 1 + S_1 S_0 D_3$, then count, for each select value, how many $(A, B)$ pairs make the chosen input 1.
cse-2026-2-cs-49.given: Decoder Q: $D_0 = \bar A \bar B$, $D_1 = \bar A B$, $D_2 = A \bar B$, $D_3 = AB$ (active high). MUX M inputs: $I_0 = D_0$, $I_1 = 0$, $I_2 = 1$, $I_3 = D_3$; selects $S_1 S_0$.

steps.title: S1S0 = 00 → Y = D0
steps.body: $Y = D_0 = \bar A \bar B$, which is 1 only for $AB = 00$ → **1** combination.

steps.title: S1S0 = 01 → Y = 0
steps.body: Input 1 is tied to 0, so no $(A,B)$ gives $Y = 1$ → **0** combinations.

steps.title: S1S0 = 10 → Y = 1
steps.body: Input 2 is tied to 1, so all four $(A,B)$ pairs give $Y = 1$ → **4** combinations.

steps.title: S1S0 = 11 → Y = D3
steps.body:
$Y = D_3 = AB$, which is 1 only for $AB = 11$ → **1** combination.

Total: $1 + 0 + 4 + 1 = 6$.

cse-2026-2-cs-49.shortcut: Each MUX input contributes (number of 1s in its function of $A, B$): a minterm gives 1, constant 0 gives 0, constant 1 gives 4 → $1 + 0 + 4 + 1 = 6$.
pitfalls: Thinking the answer depends on whether A or B is the decoder MSB — $D_0$ (00) and $D_3$ (11) are the same either way.
Counting only select values (gives 3 of 4 select codes) instead of full $[A\,B\,S_1\,S_0]$ combinations.
Treating the decoder as active low (would swap the roles: $D_0$ true for 3 pairs).
cse-2026-2-cs-49.verification: $Y = S_1\bar S_0 + \bar S_1 \bar S_0 \bar A \bar B + S_1 S_0 AB$: the three terms are disjoint with $4 + 1 + 1 = 6$ minterms out of 16.

cse-2026-2-cs-50.approach: Trace the program line by line, keeping a table of the variables and of what `ptr` points to. Every write through `*ptr` changes the variable `ptr` currently points at.

steps.title: Initialise the variables
steps.body: Line 3 sets $a = 5$, $b = 11$, $c = 20$. `ptr` is not yet pointing anywhere.

steps.title: Write c into a through ptr
steps.body:
Line 4: `ptr = &a`, so `*ptr` **is** `a`.

Line 5: `*ptr = c` stores $20$ into `a`: now $a = 20$.

steps.title: Re-point ptr and copy b into a
steps.body:
Line 6: `ptr = &c`, so `*ptr` is now `c`.

Line 7: `a = *(&b)` — `&b` is b's address and `*` undoes it, so this is just `a = b`: $a = 11$.

steps.title: Compute c and print it
steps.body:
Line 8: `c = *ptr - a` reads `*ptr` (which is `c` = 20) **before** assigning: $c = 20 - 11 = 9$.

Line 9 prints **9**.

cse-2026-2-cs-50.shortcut: Ignore the pointer noise: `*ptr = c` makes $a = 20$, `a = *(&b)` makes $a = 11$, and `*ptr` at the end is `c` itself, so $c = 20 - 11$.
pitfalls: Thinking `*ptr = c` changes `c` — it changes whatever `ptr` points to (here `a`).
Using the old $a = 20$ in the last line; `a` was overwritten with 11 on line 7.
cse-2026-2-cs-50.verification: Rewrite without pointers: `a = c; a = b; c = c - a;` → $a = 20$, $a = 11$, $c = 20 - 11 = 9$.
